name: Collagen peptides
summary: Collagen is a structural protein in connective tissues. Collagen peptide supplements contain collagen broken into smaller protein fragments, usually from animal tissues. They supply amino acids but are not a complete protein source.
commonUses: May improve skin elasticity and wrinkles
May help keep muscle and bone as you age
roles: Collagen is part of the structural framework of skin, cartilage, bones and tendons.
Collagen is rich in glycine and proline but has an incomplete essential amino acid profile; it is not nutritionally interchangeable with a complete protein.

status.note: This basic guide does not provide a routine status test.

low.note: Collagen is not an essential nutrient: the body makes it from amino acids. No deficiency condition or required intake has been established.

high.note: See the cautions below; this guide does not establish a safe upper amount.

examples: Skin, bones, tendons and cartilage of meat, poultry and fish
foodSources.note: Collagen only occurs in animal connective tissue, so plant foods have none. Eating collagen-rich foods is different from taking hydrolysed collagen peptides.

forms.name: Hydrolysed collagen or collagen peptides
forms.note: Collagen broken into smaller fragments. The source animal and processing method affect the mixture of peptides.

forms.name: Gelatin
forms.note: Heat-denatured collagen, with different physical properties from a collagen peptide powder.

forms.name: Undenatured collagen
forms.note: Retains more of its original structure and is a different preparation from hydrolysed collagen. The products are not interchangeable.

reference.noUpperLimit: No tolerable upper intake level was found for collagen peptides in general. EFSA (2025) judged egg membrane collagen peptides, a different product, safe up to 500 mg a day in food supplements for adults other than pregnant and breastfeeding women. That does not apply to bovine, porcine or marine collagen.

sources.title: Safety of egg membrane collagen peptides as a novel food

cautions: Check the source animal: collagen may come from cattle, pigs, chickens, fish or other marine organisms. The word marine does not identify the species or its allergy suitability.
With a fish allergy, discuss a fish-derived collagen product with an allergy clinician rather than assuming processing makes it suitable. Check the full ingredient and allergen information.
Collagen is not a nutritionally complete replacement for other dietary protein sources.
Long-term safety information is limited for the many different peptide products. A study of one preparation does not establish the safety of every collagen blend.

origin: Collagen is the main structural protein of skin, tendons, cartilage and bone. Collagen peptide supplements are made by heating and breaking down (hydrolysing) collagen from the skin, bones or scales of cattle, pigs, chickens or fish.
Labels often name collagen types such as I and III. This guide has not compared types, and the source animal, processing method and any added ingredients such as vitamin C differ between products.
dosage: No reference intake or upper limit has been set. Products differ in grams per serving, source and added ingredients, and a study of one product does not carry over to every other.
Amounts commonly used in studies and supplements are about 11 to 22 g a day of hydrolysed collagen peptides. This is not a reference intake or a personal recommendation.

Check the grams of collagen per serving and the source animal on the label, and avoid adding together several products. Results for a mixture, such as collagen with vitamin C, cannot be credited to collagen alone.

foodAmounts.verdict: Partly. Collagen-rich foods such as skin, bones, gelatin and bone broth contain collagen, but this guide has no checked per-food figures, so it cannot say how much of any food matches the 11–22 g commonly used in supplements. Digestion also breaks food collagen into amino acids and small peptides, and hydrolysed supplements are already broken down, so food and supplement are not the same intervention.
foodAmounts.notChecked: This guide has no checked collagen figures per food, so it does not list how much of each food would give a set amount.
